example:
ds = DisjointSet(4)
ds.union(0, 1)
ds.union(2, 3)
ds.union(1, 2)
ds.union(0, 3)
start: Give every machine a note naming another machine, and let one machine per group name itself: the group's representative. Two machines are connected exactly when following their notes ends at the same representative, and joining two groups only needs one representative's note to change.

A disjoint-set forest: `parent[v]` starts as `v`, and `find` follows parents up to the root. `union` finds both roots, returns `False` when they are the same, and otherwise hangs the smaller tree's root under the larger's, counts one component fewer, and returns `True`. What stays true: from any vertex the parent links end at exactly one root, and two vertices are connected exactly when their roots match.

start.text: The tests also read `ds.parent` and `ds.components` directly, and after `find` they expect every vertex it walked through to point straight at the root. The shape, with the walking and linking left to you:

test_join_duplicate_and_identity: On 4 vertices: `union(0, 1)` is `True`, `union(1, 0)` is `False` because they already share a component, `connected(2, 2)` is `True`, `connected(0, 2)` is `False`, and `ds.components` must be `3`. `union` returns whether it merged two components, and `components` is an attribute holding a number, not a method.
test_against_explicit_component_sets: 80 seeded random unions on 12 vertices, some joining a vertex to itself or repeating a link. After each one it compares `union`'s result with whether two components really merged, `connected` for all 144 pairs, and `ds.components` with the true count. Only a union that merges may lower `components`.

If `connected` goes wrong after a few unions, check that `union` links the two roots, not `a` and `b` themselves: setting `parent[a] = b` when `a` is not a root cuts `a` away from the rest of its group.
test_compression_and_bounds: After `union(0, 1)`, `union(2, 3)` and `union(0, 2)`, vertex 3 can sit two links below its root. The test calls `find(3)` and checks that `ds.parent[3]` is then the root itself: `find` has to repoint every vertex it walks through, not only return the root.

`find(-1)` and `find(4)` on 4 vertices must raise `IndexError`, and a list reads `parent[-1]` without complaint, so check `0 <= v < n` yourself. Then `DisjointSet(0).components` must be `0`, and `DisjointSet(-1)` must raise `ValueError`, which `list(range(-1))` never does on its own.

AttributeError: The tests read `ds.components` and `ds.parent` directly, though the starting code does not show them. Keep the number of components in `self.components` and the parent links in `self.parent`, a list indexed by vertex.
RecursionError: A recursive `find` that never bottoms out is following parent links round a circle. Linking `a` and `b` themselves makes one: `union(0, 1)` then `union(1, 0)` leaves 0 pointing at 1 and 1 at 0. Find both roots first, and change nothing when they are the same.

stopped: A `find` loop that never ends is walking a circle of parent links. Linking the vertices instead of their roots makes one: `union(0, 1)` then `union(1, 0)` leaves 0 pointing at 1 and 1 at 0. Link the two roots, and only when they differ.

If the walk up is fine, check the loop that repoints vertices at the root: each turn must move on to the vertex's old parent, saved before you overwrite it. A turn that only sets `parent[v] = root` never moves.
passing: All passing. As your own input, make `ds = DisjointSet(20000)` on one line and time `[ds.union(i, i // 2) for i in range(1, 20000)]` on the last, then the same at 40,000. Then the README's second follow-up: a parent link is not a network link, so how would you support removing a link?
